description: The larval stage of the cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) is the most destructive phase of this pest. The caterpillars feed aggressively on leaves, buds, flowers, fruits, and seeds of many crops. Larvae vary in color from green, brown, pink, or black and usually have longitudinal stripes along the body. Because they feed directly on reproductive plant structures, they can cause significant yield losses in crops such as cotton, tomato, maize, and chickpea.
symptoms: Holes in leaves, buds, and flowers
Larvae boring into fruits or pods
Damaged cotton bolls and young fruits
Presence of frass (insect excrement) around feeding sites
Premature dropping of flowers or fruits

larva_characteristics.distinctive_features: Prominent longitudinal stripes along the body and a brown head capsule.

economic_significance: Larvae cause severe crop damage by feeding directly on reproductive plant structures. This feeding can significantly reduce yield and quality, particularly in cotton, tomato, and maize. Damage may also allow secondary infections by fungi or bacteria.

monitoring: Inspect plants regularly for eggs and young larvae
Use pheromone traps to monitor adult moth populations
Check buds, flowers, and fruits for feeding damage
cultural_control: Removal of weeds and crop residues
Deep ploughing after harvest to destroy pupae
Planting trap crops such as sunflower or marigold
mechanical_control: Removing infested fruits and plant parts
Using pheromone and light traps to monitor populations

chemical_control.note: Chemical insecticides should be used only when pest populations exceed economic thresholds and as part of an Integrated Pest Management strategy.
